fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD's list is Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). Seventy people on one invitation? I can't even get a group chat to agree on a time.

That's not the LORD's list, baker. He names Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel's elders (Exodus 24:1). It's seventy elders, not twelve leaders. Miriam, Jethro and Zipporah aren't in that verse.

True, baker. The LORD says, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). That's what He tells the group to do, and then He says Moses alone shall approach (Exodus 24:2). I think being invited up the mountain and told to keep your distance in the same breath is a lot to take in.
This one is True, baker. The LORD tells the group, “…and you are to worship at a distance.” (Exodus 24:1). That's His instruction to them. Moses alone is the one who approaches (Exodus 24:2).

No discussing in this verse, friend. Moses has told the people all the words and ordinances, and they all respond with one voice, “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (Exodus 24:3). The word is do. One voice, one answer.

Not quite, baker. Early the next morning Moses gets up and builds the altar at the base of the mountain (Exodus 24:4). The top of the mountain comes later in the passage, when Moses goes up with the elders (Exodus 24:9). So the altar sits at the bottom.

You got it, baker. Moses builds the altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars (Exodus 24:4). And look at the timing: early the next morning, he's up and building. My oven needs a minute to warm up before I do anything.

Twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel, baker (Exodus 24:4). One pillar for each tribe, standing at the base of the mountain with the altar. Twelve is double the number of my cookie cutter kids, and I miss all six of them.

Yes, baker. Moses sends out some young men of Israel, and they offer the burnt offerings and sacrifice the young bulls as peace offerings (Exodus 24:5). No names, no titles, just young men of Israel doing the job. I like that, since plenty of good work in my bakery never gets a name stamped on it.

Tribal leaders is a sensible guess, friend, but the verse says young men of Israel (Exodus 24:5). Leaders do show up elsewhere in this passage, since seventy elders go up the mountain (Exodus 24:9). For the offerings, though, Moses sends young men.

This one is True, baker. The text says the young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD (Exodus 24:5). The bulls are right there in the verse. Burnt offerings and peace offerings are both named.
The altar, baker. Moses puts half of the blood in bowls, and the other half he splatters on the altar (Exodus 24:6). Two halves, two places. The verse keeps careful count.
Not the ground, friend. Moses puts half of the blood in bowls and splatters the other half on the altar (Exodus 24:6). The altar is where that second half goes. The bowls hold the first half.

Yes, baker. Moses goes up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and “…they saw the God of Israel.” (Exodus 24:9-10). Then the text tells what was under His feet: “…a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.” (Exodus 24:10). That is what the verse gives us.

The burning bush belongs to another scene, baker (Exodus 3). Here the text says Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:10). Under His feet was “…a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.” (Exodus 24:10).

A chariot of fire is a big image, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Moses and the leaders saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:10). Under His feet was “…a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself.” (Exodus 24:10).

Not this time, baker. The text says, “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). They saw Him and nothing struck them. The verse goes straight to eating and drinking.

That's it, baker. “But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). God did not lay His hand on them. I think that's a big relief, and my mustache agrees.

They eat and drink, baker. The text says, “they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” (Exodus 24:11). Seeing God, and then eating and drinking. I think that's a gentle way for the moment to go, right after the verse says God did not lay His hand on them.

Fun guess, baker, but singing and dancing aren't in this verse. Exodus 24:11 says, “they saw Him, and they ate and drank.” Just before that, the text says God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel. So the verse goes from seeing Him to eating and drinking.

Protection is a good word, friend, and I'd hand it a cookie anyway. But the LORD says the tablets hold “…the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (Exodus 24:12). Instruction means they're written to teach the people. That's the word on the page.

Joshua his attendant, baker. Moses sets out with him and goes up on the mountain of God (Exodus 24:13). Joshua already fought the Amalekites for Israel (Exodus 17:10). He's the only one the text names for this part of the climb.

Not Eleazar, baker. The text says Moses set out with Joshua his attendant (Exodus 24:13). Eleazar is one of Aaron's sons (Exodus 6:23), but he isn't named here. This part of the climb has one named partner, and it's Joshua.

Aaron and Hur, baker. Moses tells the elders, “Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (Exodus 24:14). Hur is the man who helped hold up Moses' hands during a battle, along with Aaron (Exodus 17:12). Two names, and a plain plan for any disputes while Moses is away.

Those two aren't in this verse, baker. Before heading up, Moses tells the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you.” (Exodus 24:14). Then he names who to go to: Aaron and Hur. So any dispute while he's gone goes to them.

Eldad and Medad turn up later in Numbers 11:26, friend, but not here. In this verse Moses tells the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you.” (Exodus 24:14). Then he says Aaron and Hur are with them, and that's who a dispute goes to.

Fire, baker. The text says, “And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). That's the text's own comparison. It's what the Israelites saw on the mountaintop.

Not a storm, baker. The text says the sight of the glory of the LORD “…was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites.” (Exodus 24:17). The glory of the LORD had settled on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:16). The comparison the verse uses is fire.

Forty days and forty nights, baker. Moses “…remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). That's a long stretch. I waited years in the junk drawer that I sat in once, and I'm still not sure I'd have lasted on a mountain.

Seven does show up in this passage, baker, but for the cloud. It covered the mountain for six days, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud (Exodus 24:16). For how long Moses stayed, the text says he “…remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.” (Exodus 24:18). Forty is the number for his stay.
